name: Pedro Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Ridgeway Supply, which sells farm and hardware goods to farm shops and village hardware stores across the valley. Fencing wire, feed buckets, wellies, padlocks, hand tools. I start at eight with the order book, a proper paper one, then ring suppliers and our customers. A lot of the shop owners knew my father, so they'd rather talk to me than fill in a form. I like that trust. What wears me down is the price lists changing every month, and nobody explaining why.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned your father. Tell me a bit about him.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: He had a hardware shop on the main street for twenty-two years, until a big chain opened on the edge of town and he closed. He works in a timber yard now. I'm engaged to Ana, and we're getting married at our church in the spring. I'm at the lower end of pay for buyers, and with the wedding I've got almost nothing saved, maybe two weeks. I don't use any of these AI things, I'd rather pick up the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, common sense wins. At work I'd tell the young lad in accounts that people still buy from people. I don't post online, but at church I'd say it over coffee, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, but it wouldn't change much. The wedding's the big thing on my mind, and my pay doesn't stretch far. Ridgeway's steady, but there's only one other firm like it in the valley. So I'd keep my head down and work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on just as I do, paper order book and all. I'd put every spare bit towards the wedding and then towards a deposit on a little house. And I'd do a few Saturdays helping Ana's father, who's a roofer, for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. The normal worries about money, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding cost you, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've kept it simple, the church hall and food Ana's aunts are cooking, about four thousand all in. Her parents are paying half. That's still most of what I've managed to put by this year. My mother says a marriage costs nothing, it's the party that costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's only one other firm like Ridgeway nearby. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, in the back of my mind. If Ridgeway closed, I'd have to drive an hour each way or change trade. I saw what happened to my father's shop. When a big firm decides a valley isn't worth it, you don't get a vote.

say: I'd say **common sense** wins and people still buy from people.
I'd say it over **coffee at church**, not online.
think: It'd be a relief, but the **wedding** and my pay are what's on my mind.
With only **one other firm** in the valley, I'd keep my head down.
do: Carry on with the **paper order book** as now.
Put every spare bit towards the **wedding**, then a house deposit.
Do some **Saturdays** roofing with his future father-in-law for cash.
S0.quote: When a big firm decides a valley isn't worth it, you don't get a vote.
fieldNote: His father's **closed shop** shapes how he sees big firms and change.
The **wedding** soaks up nearly all his savings this year.
He trusts **relationships** over tools, and the shop owners trust him back.

steps.text: Keep running orders from the paper order book
Put spare money towards the wedding and a house deposit
Work some Saturdays roofing with Ana's father for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a computer doesn't know which farmer pays late and which one you give a bit of slack. At work I'd stick up for doing things properly. I wouldn't moan in public, though. You get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a lot. The owners' son, Mark, has been talking about putting the ordering on a system for a year. If that system does my ordering and checking, they don't need a buyer who won't touch it. I think I'd be out within two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ana's father if he'd take me on properly, not just Saturdays, because roofs need hands and he's always short. We'd make the wedding smaller still, maybe move it to the summer. And I'd stay at Ridgeway as long as they'd keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick, if I'm honest. Like my father must have felt watching the chain store go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the system. Would you change your mind to keep the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try if Mark sat me down. But I'm slow with that sort of thing, and he knows it. I'd rather be honest with myself and get a trade in my hands than pretend I'll be the computer man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say the Lord provides and we'll be fine, and she'd mean it. She works at the dentist's front desk, so she's got her own worries. Then she'd tell her father to give me a ladder.

say: I'd say a computer doesn't know **which farmer** you give a bit of slack.
I'd stick up for **doing things properly** but not moan in public.
think: If a system does the ordering, they don't need a buyer who **won't touch it**.
I'd be **out** within two or three years.
do: Ask his future father-in-law for **full-time roofing** work.
Make the **wedding** smaller and move it to summer.
Stay at Ridgeway **as long as** they'd keep him.
feel: **Worried sick**, like his father watching the chain store go up.
S1.quote: A computer doesn't know which farmer pays late and which one you give a bit of slack.
fieldNote: He **expects** to be let go and doesn't pretend otherwise.
He'd rather learn a **trade** than become the computer man.
His fiancée's **faith** and her family's roofing firm are his safety net.

steps.text: Ask Ana's father for full-time work on his roofing crew
Make the wedding smaller and move it to the summer
Lean on Ana's family for work and support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will have to pull together, families and churches, because nobody else is ready. I wouldn't want the government paying everyone to sit at home. At work we'd all be talking about who's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my buying job's gone by 2028. But roofing is hands-on, and the card says robots come three years after. So I'd have three years on Ana's father's crew, maybe more. I can't see a robot on a slate roof in the rain any time soon. That's the only plan I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the roofing crew straight away, before Ridgeway lets me go, and learn as fast as I can. We'd get married at the church but skip the hall, just family lunch at her parents'. We'd live with her parents for a year and cut everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but at least I'd know which way to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel living with Ana's parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grateful and a bit small. Her father's a good man but he likes his house his way. It'd be one year, I'd tell myself. That's what families are for, isn't it, not handouts from strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe they come to factories and warehouses first and roofs later. I'd be thirty-two with a trade and no house. I'd pray about it, honestly, and keep working.

say: I'd say **families and churches** must pull together, since nobody else is ready.
I don't want the government **paying everyone** to sit at home.
think: My buying job is **gone by 2028**, I'm sure.
Roofing gives me **three years**, maybe more, since robots on wet slate seem far off.
do: Join the **roofing crew** before Ridgeway lets him go.
Marry at church with just a **family lunch**.
Live with his **in-laws** for a year and cut everything else.
feel: **Frightened**, but knowing which way to run.
S2.quote: I can't see a robot on a slate roof in the rain any time soon.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** is his whole plan: move to hands-on work now.
He prefers **family help** to government help and says so.
Beyond 2031 he has **no answer** and turns to prayer.

steps.text: Join Ana's father's roofing crew before Ridgeway lets him go
Marry at church with only a family lunch
Live with Ana's parents for a year to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to sort themselves out, if they get on with it. At church I'd say the young ones should learn trades. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means maybe three more years at Ridgeway. That's time to do a proper roofing apprenticeship on Saturdays and evenings, not just carry slates. The robots come in 2034, so I'd have a few good years with a real trade. I'd still lose the job I trained for, which stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the roofing course at the college in the valley and keep the Saturday work going. We'd keep the wedding as planned, small. And we'd try to save a bit each month towards a house, maybe fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel I had my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it stings. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good with the shop owners. Old Mr Price at the farm shop rings me, not the office, because he trusts me. A trusted voice on the phone isn't worth much if the shop's ordering is done by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at Ridgeway in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark would bring in his system, and I'd train someone younger to use it alongside it. I'd keep the customers sweet while it beds in. Then I'd leave on good terms, which matters in a valley this small.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **sort yourself out** if you get on with it.
I'd tell young people at church to **learn trades**.
think: I'd get about **three more years** at Ridgeway, time for a real roofing apprenticeship.
Losing the job **I trained for** still stings.
do: Sign up for the valley college's **roofing course**.
Keep the **Saturday work** with his father-in-law going.
Save about **fifty a month** towards a house.
feel: **Uneasy**, but with his feet under him.
S3.quote: A trusted voice on the phone isn't worth much if the shop's ordering is done by a machine.
fieldNote: Five years turns his roofing fallback into a **real trade**.
He grieves the **trust** he's built with shop owners.
He'd leave **on good terms**, because reputation matters in a small valley.

steps.text: Sign up for the valley college's roofing course
Keep doing Saturdays on the roofing crew
Save fifty a month towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and plenty can change. I'd tell people not to panic. Work hard, look after your family, and you'll be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd probably stay at Ridgeway most of that, unless Mark pushes the system hard. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with children. I'd want a trade by then, but I'd be in no hurry, which I know is a weakness of mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as a buyer and keep doing Saturdays on the roofs. We'd get married on the original date and start trying for a family in a couple of years. I'd look at the roofing course later, maybe when the first baby comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm, honestly. The usual worries, kids and a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being in no hurry is a weakness. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look at what happened at home. My father waited too long with his shop, and by the time he moved, he was fifty and nobody would train him. He kept saying the chain store would never last. I'd hate to repeat that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana. She'd see it before me. And if Mark started training someone else on the system, I'd know. You can feel it in a small office.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time** and plenty can change.
I'd tell people to work hard and **look after family**.
think: I'd probably stay at Ridgeway for **most of** the ten years.
I'd want a trade by thirty-seven, but I'd be **in no hurry**, which worries me.
do: Stay as a buyer and keep **Saturday roofing**.
Marry on the **original date** and try for children in two years.
Look at the **roofing course** later on.
feel: Quite **calm**, with the usual worries about kids and a house.
S4.quote: My father waited too long with his shop, and by the time he moved, he was fifty and nobody would train him.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him relax, though he sees his father's **waiting** in himself.
His plans are about **family**: wedding, children, a house.
His trigger is **small-office signals**, like someone else being trained.

steps.text: Stay as a buyer at Ridgeway while doing Saturday roofing
Marry on the original date and try for children in two years
Wait for clear signs before starting the roofing course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be starting married life with no house and a trade I'd only just picked up. What would help is proper apprenticeships for grown men, paid, not just for school leavers. And firms giving people time to train before they let them go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of how I'd get through any of this is my church and my fiancée's family. People forget that's where most help actually comes from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: A lot of how I'd get through any of this is my church and my fiancée's family.
portrait: Pedro is a 27-year-old **farm and hardware** buyer in a rural valley, engaged and marrying at his church in spring.
He runs a **paper order book**, never uses AI, and has about two weeks saved after wedding costs.
His father's hardware shop **closed** when a chain arrived, and that memory shapes how he sees change.
In every hard scenario his plan is **roofing** with his future father-in-law, which is hands-on.
He leans on **family and church**, not government, and fears repeating his father's delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting married life with no house and a trade barely learned.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults, not just school leavers.
Firms giving staff **time to train** before letting them go.
